newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's economy stumbles into reverse in Q1 1997.
newsitem.headline: Italy's economy stumbles into reverse in Q1 1997.

text.p: Italy's economy lurched into reverse during the first quarter of 1997, with growth contracting by a surprisingly sharp year-on-year rate of 0.5 percent, official data showed on Friday.

Gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 0.3 percent compared with the final quarter of 1996, the second quarterly decline in a row, provisional figures released by national statistics institute Istat said.
The data come at an awkward moment for Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who is preparing to unveil his three-year plan of economic targets and growth forecasts later on Friday.

Analysts said the data were affected by fewer working days in the first three months of the year compared with the previous quarter. But they said the economy was more sluggish than expected and could technically be classified as in recession.
Economists had forecast growth would be stagnant on an annual basis, with a 0.1 percent quarter on quarter rise.
"Clearly the economy is suffering and screaming out for a fall in the discount rate," said Alex Garrard, economist at UBS in London.
Istat summarised the factors behind the fall, saying in a statement that there had been a decline in industrial output and only a slight rise in activity in the services sector.

Italy's economy was already grinding to a halt by December last year when it showed final quarter growth of a mere 0.1 percent on an annual basis but a fall of 0.2 percent compared with the preceding three-month period.
Indications so far are that the government is aiming for 1.0 to 1.2 percent GDP growth this year.

But Garrard said: "Given today's numbers Italian GDP will now need to grow by another 1.8 percent over the next three quarters in order to achieve the government's target average of 1.2 percent over the year."
Lorenzo Codogno, economist at Bank of America here, said he expected economic growth to pick up in the second quarter and rebound more significantly in the third.
"This should be sufficient to have 1.0 percent overall growth for 1997, although I think it will be difficult to reach 1.2 percent," Codogno said.

Economists said the data reinforced the pressing need for Italian interest rates to fall. Financial markets have for weeks been expecting the Bank of Italy to lop 50 to 75 basis points off the 6.75 percent discount rate.

Falling inflation -- now down to around 1.5 percent year-on-year -- and the sluggish economy have fuelled those expectations but a sudden deterioration of the lira exchange rate on the currency markets this week has dented hopes of an imminent reduction.

Analysts say the central bank is likely to wait for the result of French elections this weekend as market nervousness over the outcome of the ballot and its potential effect on plans for forming a single European currency have undermined the lira.
Codogno believed the Bank of Italy was still planning to cut rates but given uncertainty in the markets related to the single currency it would wait for several days, if not weeks.

"At this stage I would say it is likely we'll see a cut by the end of June but not maybe in the next few days. But with such a weak economic cycle and low inflation, it's pretty much overdue," Codogno added.
